link.title: घोषणापत्र, भविष्य गुमाएको देशमा राष्ट्रिय थकानको

content.$t:
छालाभित्र न्यानो सास मात्र बाँकी रहन्छ। जसरी नदी शब्दहरू नाघेर, अर्थहरू बिर्सेर, पहाड फोरेर बगेको हुन्छ, म बोल्छु, उसले सुन्छ, म हिँड्छु, उसले बाटो सम्झिन्छ। जसलाई उज्यालोले मात्र हल्लाउँछ। जसलाई छायाँले मात्र बचाइराख्छ।

छायाँमा
सत्य कुरीरहेछ, महोदय।
उज्यालोमा
हामी त्यसै झुलिरहेछौं।

संसार
उज्यालोको भाषामा बोल्छ।
छायाँले
प्रश्न गर्दैन, मात्रै पर्खन्छ।

उज्यालो
जसले छायाको मुटु चिन्दैन,
छायाँले बुझ्छ
उज्यालो मात्रै एक सजावट हो।

घामले
कुरा गर्दैन, केवल देखाउँछ।
म बुझेको नाटकमा
आफ्ना आँखा बन्द गरिदिन्छु।

कहिलेकाहीँ
अन्धकारको गहिराइ बिर्सिएरै
आँखाको उज्यालो नाप्न खोज्दा
आफ्नै मुटुका घाउहरूलाई नै
म फूलहरूको रूपक बनाईरहेको भेट्छु।

सत्य
त्यो मुक्ति, त्यो रोग,
जो आफ्नै प्रतिबिम्बमा हराउँछ,
जुन आफ्नो स्वीकृतिमा मर्छ।

एकै
शरीरका दुई मौनता,
एउटा प्रश्न बनेर बाँचिरहेको,
अर्को जवाफ भएर हराइरहेको।

सन्तुलन
त्यसरी नै टिकाइरहेको हुन्छु,
जसरी
म हराइरहेको हुन्छु।

हरेक दिन
थोरै उज्यालो मर्छ,
थोरै अन्धकार बाँच्छ।
न नाममा, न इतिहासमा,
न मुटुका ती कुनामा।

छालाभित्र
न्यानो सास मात्र बाँकी रहन्छ।

जसरी नदी
शब्दहरू नाघेर, अर्थहरू बिर्सेर,
पहाड फोरेर बगेको हुन्छ,
म बोल्छु, उसले सुन्छ,
म हिँड्छु, उसले बाटो सम्झिन्छ।

छायाँको
न्यानोपनमा म सबै कुरा बिर्सन्छु।
उज्यालोको दायरा, विपनाको करार,
भाषाको भार, भविष्यको सूची,
आधा उज्यालो, आधा अस्वीकार,
थप शान्ति, थप एक्लोपन।

सत्य
रातको खाचोमोचामा,
छायाँको शरीरमा
नबोलेको, नसोचेको,
धेरै नजिक, अझै धेरै टाढा,
स-साना बिन्दुमा टिकेको भेट्टाउँछु।

बिन्दुले
सत्यको नजिक पुग्दा
आ-आफ्नो आकार लिन्छन्।
आकारले अन्त्य बोल्छन्।

अन्तिम सास
जसले आवाज बन्न अस्वीकार गर्छ।
हावाजस्तै
छुन नसकिने, नछोएरै पनि दुख्ने।

जसलाई
उज्यालोले मात्र हल्लाउँछ।
जसलाई
छायाँले मात्र बचाइराख्छ।

सत्य
सायद त्यही आवाज,
जसलाई कोही सुन्दैन,
जसले सबै कुरा सुन्छ।

छायाँको औँठामा
उज्यालोको
अर्को सुन्दर भ्रमभित्र,
थोरै बढी, थोरै सत्य,
छायाँको तापमा
जलिरहेका शब्दहरू।

छायाँमा
सत्य कुरीरहेछ, महोदय।
यसपटक
उज्यालो मभित्र झुलिरहेछ।

- E/A ट्रेन,
जमैका, न्युयोर्क

बासभका अरू कविता: प्रिय म, (ऐनाभित्रको पत्र) · वाद्यहरूको विरोध संगित · मौनताको चिसो · सबै कविता ›

वाद्यहरूको यो सेना उठोस्; सारंगीका तार, ढोलका ठोका, बाँसुरीका श्वासहरू एउटै तालमा मिल्छन हाम्रो सङ्गीतले कागजातमा लेखिएका दावीहरू पनि बचाउन। म सारंगी हुँ- मेरो तारबाट उठ्ने ध्वनि सुन। म ढोल हुँ- मेरो ठोकाबाट उठ्ने कदम…

म सारंगी हुँ;
मेरो तारमा लुकेको छ
थिचिएका अनुहारहरूको सास।
मेरो तालमा धड्किरहेको छ
भत्किएका सडकहरूको धुन।

मेरो तारमा अड्किएको छ;
थारु आमाको लोरी,
तामाङ दाइका गीत,
मधेसका लोकसुर,
जनजातिका बिहानी भाका।

सारंगी हुँ म;
सजावटको कोठामा झुन्ड्याएर
मलाई चुप बस्ने नबनाउ।
रेट मलाई-
ताकि सुतेका कानहरू बिउँझून्,
रेट मलाई-
ताकि भुलाइएका नामहरू उच्चरित हुन्।

म ढोल हुँ;
मलाई कुनामा थन्काएर नछोड,
धुलोको थुप्रोमुनि लुकाएर नछोड।
बजाउ मलाई-
त्यो भाकामा- जसले निदाएको गाउँ उठाओस्,
त्यो तालमा- जसले मौन सहर हल्लाओस्।

ढोल हुँ म;
म बज्दा एक्लो हुँदैन,
मेरो तालमा सयौँ हात जोडिन्छन्,
मेरो धड्कनमा हजारौँ हृदय मिसिन्छन्,
बजाउ मलाई-
मेरो आवाज सुनेर दमनका ढोकाहरू काँपून्,
डराएर अन्यायका पर्खालहरू भत्किउन।

थाह पाउन;
मेरो आवाज केवल नाचको लागि होइन,
मेरो आवाज विद्रोहको भाषा पनि हो।

बाँसुरी बन्छु म;
साँसले बोल्ने प्रमाण,
भुलेका भाषाहरूको आह्वान।
बजाउ मलाई-
मेरो स्वरले मातृभाषाको पहिचान फुकालोस्
विद्यालयको पाठ्यपुस्तकमा,
सभाको भाषामा, कानुनको शब्दमा।

बाँसुरी हुँ म;
मलाई दबाउन खोज्नेलाई
मेरो स्वरले स्मरण गराओस्:
भाषा नटुन्ने अधिकार हो।

मादल, तबला, ढल्के
हाम्रो सङ्गीतले मात्र नृत्य बल्दैन;
महिलाहरू उठ्छन्-
“आमाहरू केवल घरकै होइनन्,
हामी राष्ट्रको मेरुदण्ड हौं।”
आदिवासीहरूले चिच्याउँछन्-
“यो जमिन हाम्रो पूर्वजको रगतले रोपिएको हो।”
मधेस कराउँछ-
“हामीलाई सीमाना होइन, अधिकार चाहिन्छ।”

वाद्यहरूको यो सेना उठोस्;
सारंगीका तार, ढोलका ठोका,
बाँसुरीका श्वासहरू एउटै तालमा मिल्छन
हाम्रो सङ्गीतले कागजातमा
लेखिएका दावीहरू पनि बचाउन।

म सारंगी हुँ- मेरो तारबाट उठ्ने ध्वनि सुन।
म ढोल हुँ- मेरो ठोकाबाट उठ्ने कदम देख।

रेट मलाई- हामीलाई बजाउ-
संगीत भित्र निहित आत्माको बल लिएर,
एक दिन
तिमी पनि त्यो तालमा नाँच्नु पर्नेछ,
नाच्नुपर्ने छैन भने, कमसेकम सुन्न पर्नेछ।

- जमैका, न्युयोर्क।

बासभका अरू कविता: कोठाभित्रको मानचित्र · प्रिय म, (ऐनाभित्रको पत्र) · छायाँमा लुकेको उज्यालोको सत्य · सबै कविता ›

तिमी बुझ्नेछौ; स्थिरता असम्भव छ, तर सुन्दरता हरेक बिहान सम्भव हुन्छ। अन्ततः ऐनाले तिम्रो अनुहार बोक्दैन अब त्यहाँ, तिम्रो आत्मा झल्किन्छ; ऐनाभित्रको घामको झिल्कोमा म लुप्त हुन्छु, तिमी बाँच्छौ; अरू धेरै जन्मदिनहरूका…

(ऐनाभित्रको काल्पनिक म, ऐनाबाहिरको वास्तविक म बीचको संवाद)

आजको रात
आकाश स्थिर छ;
जुनको उज्यालो धुमिल छ
र तिमी पनि थकित छौ।

रात चकमन्न छ
कोठा चुपचाप;
भित्तेपात्रोले काँचुली फेरेसँगै
घडीहरू पनि थाकेर बसेका छन्।
भित्ताको छायाँ- एउटा अदृश्य आकृति बनेर
तिमीलाई- तिमी हुनुको आभास दिइरहन्छन्।

चिसो सतहपारि यो ऐनाभित्रैबाट
तिमीरुपी म; तिमीलाई नै हेर्दैछु।

तिमी- आफैँसँग कुरा गरिरहेका छौ
जसरी छायाँले छायाँसँग गर्छ।
म- सुनिरहेको छु, साससँग तौरिँदै
छालाभित्र चलिरहेका अधुरा संवादहरू।

सहरको कोकोहोलोको अस्तित्वविहीन हुलमा;
जब- सोचमग्न, आफ्नै अस्तित्वको खोज गर्छौ,
तब- आफ्ना हरेक गल्तीहरूको गन्ती गर्छौ।
जसरी- रुखले हरेक पतनलाई
शरदमा झरेका पातको नामले
हिउँदभरि सम्झन्छ।

म सुन्छु- तिम्रो हड्डीहरूको आवाज;
उनीहरू भन्छन्, “होस्टे, हैंसे। होस्टे, हैंसे।”

हड्डीभन्दा गहिरो ठाउँमा
एक्कासि अर्को डर पलाउँछ;
तिमी आफू बन्ने डर।

जुन डरलाई त धेरै पहिलेदेखि
तिमीले आफ्नो साथी बनाएका छौ।
जो- तिमीसँगै बस्छ, तिमीसँगै हिँड्छ,
तिम्रो काँपिरहेको छायामा,
तिम्रा ओठभित्रका सासहरूमा।

रातको सन्नाटा कोठाभरि छ;
एउटा आशाको झिनो त्यान्द्रो बोकेर;
शायद बाहिर बिहान सुरु हुँदैछ
तिमी रातको त्यही ऐनाभित्र
अझै कतै अड्किरहेको पाउँछौ।
तिम्रा अन्तर्मनका आवाजहरू म
पानीझैँ ओसिलो मौनताले भिजेका भेट्छु।

तिमी सोच्छौ;
कति जन्महरू बिर्सन बाँकी
आफ्नै गल्तीहरू सम्झँदै,
कति मरणहरू बाँच्न बाँकी
केवल विगतका उत्तर खोज्दै।
दुखाइ केवल पीडा होइन,
दुखाइ- साक्षी हो,
प्रत्येक आँसु- अर्को कविता
जसले तिमीलाई धरातल फर्काउँछ।

न्यानो, सजीव पीडाहरू;
जहाँ- आँसुले आँखाको ढुसी फुकाउँछ,
जहाँ- हरेक चोटहरूलाई जीवनले
नयाँ कविताको पानामा बदल्छ।
जहाँ- तिमी आफू नहुनुको पीडा महसुस गर्छौ,
जसले- अझै तिमीलाई जिजीविषा सिकाइरहेका छन्।

जीवनले अर्थ खोज्दैन,
मात्रै उपस्थितिको आग्रह गर्छ।
जब आत्मा निरन्तर प्रश्न गर्छ;
“के बाँच्नु नै सजाय हो?”
म ऐनाको सतहमा रगतले लेखिदिन्छु,
“तिमी यहाँ छौ। तिमी अहिले छौ।
तिमी छौ। तिमी छौ। तिमी छौ।”

तिमी उपस्थित हुन्छौ,
आफ्ना- थकानसँग, मौनतासँग,
आफ्ना- गल्तीहरू, डरहरूसँग।
न कसैले तिमीलाई बुझ्न सक्यो
न तिमीले कसैलाई बुझाउन
जीवनको गहिराइ कस्तो अनौठो!
शरीरको दुखाइ बुझाउनै नसकिने।

बिहान बिस्तारै झ्यालबाट तिमीलाई चियाएर हेर्छ,
बिहानको पहिलो घाम- पुराना घाउहरूमा पस्छ
हावा भित्रिन्छ; थकानजस्तो, तर नयाँ।

तिमी माफ गर्छौ- ती आँखाहरूलाई
जसले तिमीलाई गलत पढे,
ती हातहरूलाई- जसले तिम्रा साथ छाडे।
म ऐनाभित्रै सुन्छु
बिहानीको पहिलो आवाज;
“म माफ गर्छु आफैँलाई पनि
अघिल्ला गल्तीहरू, मौनहरू,
आकांक्षाहरू, थकानहरू
सबैलाई।”

छतमा पहिलो उज्यालो
शान्त झरेको छ।
तिमी बिस्तारै उठ्छौ;
म बसेको ऐना
तिम्रो सासले धुमिल बन्दै जान्छ।
तिम्रो नाङ्गो मनले जब बिहानीको
पहिलो शीतलाई छुन्छ,
तिमी नयाँ यात्रामा निस्कन्छौ
अर्थ नखोजी, छायाँसँग।

तिमी बुझ्नेछौ; स्थिरता असम्भव छ,
तर सुन्दरता हरेक बिहान सम्भव हुन्छ।

अन्ततः
ऐनाले तिम्रो अनुहार बोक्दैन
अब त्यहाँ, तिम्रो आत्मा झल्किन्छ;
ऐनाभित्रको घामको झिल्कोमा
म लुप्त हुन्छु, तिमी बाँच्छौ;
अरू धेरै जन्मदिनहरूका निमित्त।

जानुअघि म भन्छु;
“तिमी बाँच्न छाड्ने छैनौ,
तिमी आफू हुन छोड्ने छैनौ,
तिमीभित्रको तिमीका लागि
अनि ऐनाभित्रको मेरा लागि।”

उही
तिम्रै नाममा,
तिम्रै लागि,
तिमी स्वयम्,
ऐनाभित्रको म।

जमैका, न्युयोर्क

title.$t: Sargon of Akkad: How the Akkadians Took Power in Mesopotamia

content.$t:
How a cupbearer from Kish humbled Sumer, forged Mesopotamia's first empire, and watched a three-century drought undo it.

For centuries, the history of Mesopotamia belonged to the Sumerian city-states of the south—proud, fiercely independent, and endlessly at war over canals, borderlands, and prestige. Yet even at the height of Sumerian ambition, when the conqueror Lugal-zage-si boasted that his dominion stretched from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean Sea, another people were quietly waiting in the wings. They were the Akkadians, long treated as the junior partners in the great river-valley civilization.

Out of their ranks would step one man who led them into outright rebellion against Sumerian rule. History remembers him as Sargon—a name that in Akkadian means "the true king." With a single audacious stroke against the walls of Uruk, he would topple the old order, found the world's first true empire, and usher in the long twilight of the Sumerian age.

In short

  • In Sumerian Mesopotamia, holding cities was never enough; true legitimacy required the blessing of Enlil at his sacred seat of Nippur.
  • Lugal-zage-si of Umma unified Sumer and claimed rule "between the seas," but his overstretched empire quickly fractured into rebellion.
  • Sargon, a cupbearer from Kish of humble legend, seized Uruk in a surprise strike, humiliated Lugal-zage-si at Nippur, and founded a new imperial capital at Akkad.
  • Under Sargon and his grandson Naram-Sin, Akkadian displaced Sumerian as the living language of administration and commerce—before a three-century drought and Gutian invasions brought the empire down.

Enlil and Nippur: The Sacred Seat of Sumerian Kingship

In Sumerian legend, three great deities tower over the pantheon: An, the sky father; Enki, the wise lord of the subterranean waters; and Enlil, the god of the "between"—the air, space, and breath where divine authority resides.

During the early centuries of the third millennium BCE, the Sumerians elevated Enlil from a local city deity to the supreme god of Sumerian culture. In this age of Enlil, ruling Sumer meant far more than holding wealthy cities like Uruk or Ur; it meant holding the mandate of Enlil.

Enlil, lord of wind and air, whose blessing at Nippur conferred legitimate kingship across Sumer.

Throughout the fourth millennium BCE, Nippur was never a political powerhouse. Situated along the Euphrates, it was neither the richest nor the most heavily fortified city in the valley, and it never spawned a conquering dynasty of its own. Yet its central geographic position—roughly midway along the Euphrates' course through the heartland—made it accessible to every major city-state. Nippur's authority flowed from a far more enduring source: it was the home of Enlil, and by extension, the spiritual fountainhead of all Sumerian kingship.

The temple of Ekur in Nippur served as Enlil's earthly residence. This was no hollow ceremonial convention; Sumerian inscriptions repeatedly depict victorious kings journeying to Nippur to lay offerings before the god and claim their legitimacy. When Lugal-zage-si marched out of Umma and began subduing rival city-states—Kish, Larsa, Ur, and Uruk—raw military might was not enough. Without Enlil's sanction, his rule would remain incomplete.

Empires rose and crumbled across Mesopotamia, yet Nippur endured as the quiet city where conquerors sought divine sanction.

In the long ebb and flow of Mesopotamian history, Uruk rose, then Ur, then Akkad, then Babylon. Each in turn marched its armies to Nippur, bowed inside the Ekur, and declared itself chosen. Empires came and crumbled; Nippur endured—the quiet city that crowned the mighty and buried their ambitions beneath the sands.

Lugal-zage-si and the Dream of Ruling Between the Seas

The uprising against the hated empire of Lagash had thrust a fierce rebel to the forefront: Lugal-zage-si of Umma. Once he sacked Lagash, his momentum proved unstoppable. Working his way north along the course of the Tigris and Euphrates, he swiftly absorbed every territory Lagash had once claimed—and refused to stop at its old borders.

At the height of his triumphs, Lugal-zage-si even claimed to have conquered all the land between the "upper sea and lower sea"—meaning the Mediterranean Sea and the Persian Gulf. That boast was almost certainly an exaggeration. Up to this point in history, the Sumerians had never managed to hold distant colonies or occupy far-flung lands for long. Yet one royal inscription declares in sweeping terms:

"The great god Enlil gave the kingship of the land to him—the region from the lower sea, through the Tigris and Euphrates, to the upper sea. Thirty-two kings gathered against him, but he defeated them and smote their cities, prostrated their lords, and destroyed the whole countryside as far as the silver mines."

This was the first time a Sumerian prince had ever staked such a claim: king of the land between the seas. To the Sumerians, the upper sea marked the western edge of the known world. Even if Lugal-zage-si's reach fell short of his words, the vision of a single ruler commanding everything between the two seas lingered in the imagination of every ambitious king who followed him.

Like King Eannatum of Lagash before him, however, Lugal-zage-si committed the fatal mistake of overstretching his resources. His newly stitched-together realm was simply too vast to govern cleanly. Before long, civil strife and open rebellion flared across several Sumerian cities.

Sargon of Akkad: The Cupbearer Who Toppled Sumer

Into this season of chaos and instability stepped the other great people of Mesopotamia, finally sensing their moment to rule. Until now, they had lived as the junior partner in the shared river-valley civilization. These were the people of Akkad—and Sargon was the man who would lead them to power.

Sargon of Akkad, whose legend begins not with a crown, but with a reed basket drifting on the Euphrates.

Sargon was not of noble birth; his story does not begin with a crown. His origin legend sounds uncannily familiar to anyone raised on biblical tales. Born in the twenty-fourth century BCE to a humble mother, he was said to have been placed in a reed basket sealed with bitumen and set adrift on the river, only to be fished out and raised by a gardener working at the royal palace of Kish.

Growing up in obscurity, Sargon began his ascent as cupbearer to the king of Kish. In ancient Mesopotamia, that title meant far more than pouring wine. A cupbearer stood at the very elbow of power—trusted with the king's life, listening to counsel, learning the rhythms of court politics and the fractures beneath them. Before long, the king entrusted Sargon with a mission of the utmost secrecy.

At the time, Kish remained under the thumb of Lugal-zage-si's Sumerian empire. The Sumerian emperor was away on a distant campaign, possibly fighting far to the west in the lands of Syria. Young Sargon was handed a small band of fighters and ordered south to Uruk, where Lugal-zage-si kept his royal capital. The plan was bold to the point of recklessness: strike Uruk by surprise, knock out the imperial capital, and break Kish free from Sumerian domination.

The towering walls of Uruk must have looked daunting to Sargon and his men. Yet Lugal-zage-si had taken the bulk of his army on campaign, leaving only a thin garrison behind. The assault caught the defenders completely off guard. Sargon's men overwhelmed the watch, scaled the ramparts, and seized the city. Before reinforcements could arrive, Sargon tore down wide sections of Uruk's mighty walls—a deliberate, deeply symbolic blow aimed at the pride of Sumer.

Lugal-zage-si was furious. He marched back at speed, rallying as many as fifty subject kings according to the inscriptions. On paper, their task looked simple enough: crush the upstart forces of a single rebel city-state. We do not know the exact tactics Sargon used on the field, only the astonishing outcome—in pitched battle, Sargon's army shattered the combined might of the Sumerian empire.

Sargon captured Lugal-zage-si alive and marched him in chains through the gates of the holy city of Nippur. There, before the temple of Enlil, Sargon subjected the fallen emperor to a searing public humiliation, forcing him to wear a wooden neck stock—a heavy yoke clamped around his neck and shoulders.

Victory imagery from the Akkadian era—Sargon humiliated Lugal-zage-si at Nippur, yet remarkably spared his life.

It was a theatrical display of dominance, yet what Sargon did next set him apart from most conquerors of his age. He did not execute the old king. Remarkably, Lugal-zage-si was permitted to live and even continue governing Uruk, provided he swore an oath of loyalty to the new high king, Sargon.

The Rise of Akkad: A New Capital and a New Order

Victory over Lugal-zage-si did not merely close one man's reign—it closed an entire era. With the Sumerian coalition broken and its proudest emperor humbled, Sargon turned to building something altogether unprecedented.

Sargon refused to make Uruk, Kish, or even Nippur his royal seat. Instead, he founded a brand-new capital of his own: the city of Akkad. Akkad was a political declaration—a deliberate break from centuries of Sumerian city-state rivalries. It was a center of power that answered to Sargon of Akkad, rather than to the ancient priesthoods and patron gods of the south.

From this new capital, Sargon marched out to conquer everything his predecessors had claimed, and more. An inscription carved beneath a statue in Nippur boasts:

"Sargon, the king of Kish, triumphed in thirty-four battles over the cities, up to the edge of the seas, and destroyed their walls. He bowed down to the gods, and the gods gave him the upper land—up to the cedar forest and up to the silver mountains."

Sargon also studied the mistakes of earlier conquerors and resolved not to repeat them. Wherever his armies took a city, he made a point of demolishing its defensive walls, stripping conquered populations of the shelter needed to stage a revolt. Once his empire was secure, he performed a grand ritual to proclaim his mastery over the known world: he washed his weapons in the waters of both the Persian Gulf and the Mediterranean Sea.

When the dust of conquest settled, Sargon proved himself an able state-builder. He centralized imperial administration, standardized weights and measures, and reformed the dating system across his realm. In many respects, he looks like a forward-thinking, pragmatic ruler. Yet Sargon was also, by any modern measure, an Akkadian nationalist.

He took a new royal title—King of Akkad—and placed fellow Akkadians in the empire's key offices. For centuries, Sumerian had stood unchallenged as the official language of royal inscriptions on palaces and temples across Mesopotamia. Under Sargon, Akkadian entered official royal inscriptions for the very first time. The ancient cuneiform script was adapted and re-engineered to record the Semitic sounds of Akkadian. Administration shifted steadily into Akkadian, while Sumerian retreated into the sacred sphere of temples, ritual, and scholarship.

The two peoples of Mesopotamia, who had lived, farmed, and built side by side for thousands of years, were beginning to drift apart. In the southern Sumerian-speaking cities, resentment simmered until it reached a boiling point.

Sargon reigned for fifty-five years, and in the twilight of his life that simmering anger exploded into a full-scale uprising. A later Babylonian chronicle preserves the memory:

"In his old age, all the lands revolted against him, and they besieged him in Akkad the city. But he went forth to battle and defeated them. He knocked them over and destroyed their vast armies."

Sargon's sheer flair for war held the empire together as long as he drew breath, yet as the aging monarch weakened, virtually every southern city burst into open revolt. When Sargon died around 2284 BCE, it fell to his two sons to inherit—and somehow contain—the storm he left behind.

The first son, Rimush, ruled for nine bloody years, spending nearly all of them fighting bitter campaigns to reconquer the rebellious Sumerian south. He crushed uprisings in Ur, Umma, Lagash, and Adab; one year of his reign entered history under the grim name "the year that Adab was destroyed." When Rimush died, Sargon's other son, Manishtushu, took the throne, reportedly falling back on the same harsh tactics of terror that had once made the old empire of Lagash so detested.

It took Sargon's grandson, Naram-Sin, to restore the Akkadian Empire to its former brilliance. He quelled the southern heartlands and returned the realm to stability. Yet Naram-Sin understood that force alone could not bind Mesopotamia together. Breaking with his grandfather's narrower title, "King of Akkad," he adopted a more diplomatic style: King of Sumer and Akkad—a deliberate gesture of reconciliation between the two halves of his empire.

A Cosmopolitan Empire and the Twilight of Spoken Sumerian

Still, even Naram-Sin could not fully mend the cultural shift already underway. The Sumerians were no longer the dominant creative engine of the region. For generations, Akkadian had been quietly overtaking Sumerian in the streets and marketplaces. Official imperial preference played its part, of course, but the deeper cause lay in the cosmopolitan makeup of the empire itself.

Sumerian was a language isolate—its grammar, structure, and sounds bore no kinship to any neighboring tongue. By contrast, the peoples living across the surrounding lands spoke languages closely related to Akkadian, all belonging to the wider Semitic language family. They shared similar grammatical roots, familiar patterns, and overlapping vocabulary. For travelers, merchants, and migrants entering Mesopotamia, picking up Akkadian was rather like an English speaker learning French, whereas Sumerian felt altogether alien—more like trying to learn Bengali from scratch.

Re-engineered from Sumerian cuneiform, Akkadian became the natural lingua franca of trade, diplomacy, and empire.

Because Akkadian was so much easier for outsiders to learn, it naturally became the lingua franca of trade, diplomacy, and daily commerce. Mesopotamia had been largely bilingual for centuries, but the balance now tipped decisively. Gradually, every Sumerian had to learn Akkadian, while fewer and fewer Akkadians saw any need to learn Sumerian.

Slowly, quietly, spoken Sumerian began to slip out of living history. Priests and scholars would preserve it inside temples and ziggurats as a sacred tongue of liturgy and learning for another two thousand years—much as Latin endured in medieval Europe—but its days as a spoken mother tongue were drawing to a close.

A Lonely Comet, a Great Drought, and the Fall of Akkad

Yet the days of the Akkadian Empire were numbered as well. When the great Naram-Sin died, the throne passed to his son, Shar-Kali-Sharri—the great-grandson of Sargon of Akkad. In the fourth year of his reign, a lonely cosmic traveler blazed across the Mesopotamian sky. Comet Hale-Bopp appeared in Earth's night sky for the first time in 2213 BCE and lingered visibly overhead for eighteen months.

In Mesopotamia—and across much of the ancient world—what followed was a relentless, devastating drought. Rainfall plummeted, and this dry spell was no passing bad season; it dragged on for centuries, leaving a scar across the globe. Climate historians link this same arid crisis to the collapse of Egypt's Old Kingdom and the decline of the Indus Valley civilization.

Extended drought ended Mesopotamia's age of grain surpluses, emptying northern towns and unraveling Sargon's empire.

With year after year of scarce rain, Mesopotamia's golden age of food surpluses came to an abrupt end. Towns and cities in the drier north began to empty out. When King Shar-Kali-Sharri died in 2193 BCE, the empire tumbled into bitter civil war and chaos.

The prolonged drought also pushed a nomadic mountain people from the north—the Guti—down into the Mesopotamian plains. They swept into the weakened heartland and burned Sargon's proud capital of Akkad so thoroughly that archaeologists have never found its ruins. For the next hundred and fifty years, the Guti would hold Mesopotamia in a bleak, fractured dark age.

History still held one final act for the Sumerians. Once the long shadow of the Gutian dark age lifted, they would rise again to lead a brief, radiant renaissance across the valley. Yet the very environment that had once birthed their civilization was already turning against them—slowly, relentlessly preparing to reclaim the land and every great city that had ruled it for ages.

म सीता, म माटोकी छोरी, अझै वनवासी, अझै प्रश्नवाची। कहिले जनकपुर, कहिले अयोध्या, कहिले वनवास, कहिले ऋषिको कुटी; म कहिल्यै घरकी भइन। कसरी प्रमाणित गरूँ - म यही माटोकी छोरी? कसरी देखाउँ तिमीलाई - मेरो गर्भमा हुर्किएको पीडा?

मधुबनको माटोमा हुर्किएकी
मिथिलाकी छोरी म।
तिमी परदेशी -
मैले मागिनँ,
मैले रोजिनँ,
मेरो प्रेम थिएन,
म जितिएकी थिएँ,
धनुषवाणको पुरुषार्थमा;
म मात्र पुरस्कार बनेँ,
विजेताको, विजेताहरूका कुलको।

बारीका फूल -
माटोको सुगन्ध,
माटोसँगै हुर्केका सपना छाडेर,
आफ्नै बगैँचाबाट टाढा–टाढा,
म दुलही भएर आएकी थिएँ -
मर्यादा पुरुषोत्तम राम,
तिम्रो विदेशी राजमहलमा।
तिम्रो साथले मलाई
वनवासको एकान्त दियो,
अपहरणको अँध्यारोमा बाँधेर
रावणको बगैँचा पुर्‍यायो।

त्यसपछि -
युद्धको गाथा,
हतियारको गर्जन,
वीरहरूको कथा।
तिमी युद्ध जितेर
फर्कियौ सिंहासनमा;
मलाई कुरेर बसिरहेका थिए
पुरुषसत्ताका शंकालु प्रश्न -
“के सीताले आफ्नो सतित्व
बचाएर राखी होली त?”
अग्निपरीक्षामा भष्म भएर
मैले साबित गर्नुपर्‍यो -
“म पवित्र छु!”

तिमीले त -
शंकाको आगोमा जलेर
मलाई जंगलवासी बन्न
बाध्य पारेका थियौ।
तिमी, त्यो धोबी, पुरुष -
शंका र अपमानले थाकेर
गर्भमा दुई प्रश्न -
लव र कुश बोकेर
म फेरि एकपटक
प्रवासी बनेकी थिएँ।

जंगलमै जन्मिए लव र कुश,
माटो भित्रैबाट उम्रीएका नामहरू,
माटोको घर, माटोकै गन्ध,
माटोकै कोखबाट जन्मिए पनि
बुवा र देश -
दुवै नखुलेका आत्मा।

राम -
म तिमीलाई प्रश्न गर्छु;
तिमीले के कहिल्यै सोच्यौ -
रावणले अपहरण गर्दा मेरो आँसु कहाँ खसे?
मैले मात्र किन दिनुपर्‍यो -
तिमीलाई पवित्रताको प्रमाणपत्र?
लव र कुशलाई जन्मनासाथ -
किन राज्यविहीन बनाएका थियौ?
तिम्रो उत्तराधिकारी बन्न -
किन पितृवंशको कागज देखाउनुपर्ने?

म सीता,
म माटोकी छोरी,
अझै वनवासी, अझै प्रश्नवाची।
कहिले जनकपुर,
कहिले अयोध्या,
कहिले वनवास,
कहिले ऋषिको कुटी;
म कहिल्यै घरकी भइन।
कसरी प्रमाणित गरूँ -
म यही माटोकी छोरी?
कसरी देखाउँ तिमीलाई -
मेरो गर्भमा हुर्किएको पीडा?

मन्दिरका ढुङ्गामा त
म स्त्री-शक्ति हुँ,
लेख्छन् धर्मग्रन्थहरूमा -
सीता शुद्ध, सीता पवित्र,
सीता सहनशील;
देशकी छोरी - देवी - माता -
मेरो आँसुमा पवित्रता खोजिन्छ,
मेरो देशमा मेरै छोराहरूलाई
विदेशी लेखिन्छ?

राजाले प्रेम दिएन,
धर्मग्रन्थले न्याय दिएन,
आज कानुनले पनि ओठ टोक्यो।
कसरी बुझ्न सकिन्थ्यो -
देशको परिभाषा यति साँघुरो होला?
जन्म दिनुअघि थाहा हुँदैन -
मातृत्व एकदिन अपराध हुनेछ।

मायाले जन्मिएका - लव र कुशहरूलाई
नियमको कागजले अस्वीकृत गरिरहन्छ।
राम र धोबीहरूले लेखेका
संविधानका पानाले
अझै भनिरहन्छ -
“विदेशीकी श्रीमती।”
“अब जन्मने तिम्रा छोराहरू
उसैको देशका हुने भए।”

बासभका अरू कविता: म प्रश्न सोध्ने माटो · घाम र फूलको प्रेम गीत · उसका लागि कविता · सबै कविता ›

म पनि- सपना देख्थें देशको, नक्शा होइन, अनुहार भएको देश। जहाँ कविले बन्दुक होइन, कलम बोकेर गर्थे प्रतिवाद। जहाँ सपना- सिर्जनाको गर्भ, सिर्जना- विद्रोहको आवाज। तर मेरो सपना हरायो! हरायो- काठमाडौंको कन्क्रिट क्यानभासमा।…

म पनि-
सपना देख्थें देशको,
जहाँ भोकले होइन,
भविष्यले झस्किन्थ्यो बालक।
जहाँ बाल-बालिकाहरूले
कुर्न पर्दैनथ्यो
अब बाँच्ने पालो।

म पनि-
सपना देख्थें देशको,
नक्शा होइन,
अनुहार भएको देश।
जहाँ कविले बन्दुक होइन,
कलम बोकेर
गर्थे प्रतिवाद।

जहाँ सपना-
सिर्जनाको गर्भ,
सिर्जना-
विद्रोहको आवाज।

तर मेरो
सपना हरायो!
हरायो- काठमाडौंको
कन्क्रिट क्यानभासमा।
जहाँ सडक चिल्लिन्छ
र सपना चिप्लिन्छ।

जहाँ सँधै-
झिल्के सतहले घाम च्यात्छ
आकाशले आफैँलाई -आफ्नो
प्रतिविम्बमा चिन्दैन,
अनि साँझसम्म-
ट्राफिक बत्तीझैँ नभनी निभ्छ।

जहाँ सँधै-
कालो सिसा भएका नेताको गाडी
जनताको पसिना मिच्दै
जनताको छायामा गुड्छन्।
जसको गन्तव्य सधैं
सिंहदरबार हुन्छ।

यहाँ आज-
सपना बेच्नेहरू सिंहदरबारमा छन्:
चाउरिएको झन्डा,
झुटा नाराको पर्दा।
रातभर चिच्याएका
नाराहरू बिहानै
संसदको हीटरमा-
चुप लाग्छन्,
ओइलाइजान्छन,
तापिइरहन्छन विद्रोहशून्य।

अब सिंहदरबारभित्र-
न सपना छ, न देशको गन्ध।
छ केवल-
नेताको भाषण,
जसको पानामा
हामी देश खोजिरहन्छौं।

जहाँ अहिले-
“जनता” शब्द,
सन्दर्भविहीन बिम्ब भएको छ-
जसको अर्थ छैन,
केवल नारा बनेर बाँच्छ;
शान्तिको नाममा
युद्धको सपना बेचिन्छ
अनि चुपचाप पचाइन्छ।

अब जनतासँग-
न देश, न सपना,
न भरोसा।
के बाँकी छ?

छ त केवल-
सम्झनामा बचेको
एक पुरानो कविता,
एक पुरानो झरी,
एक पुरानो देश
अपुरो बिलौना।

अब म-
देश सम्झिंदा भेट्छु
कविको काँधमा चुँडिएको
सपनाको घाँटी,
बाँच्न नपाएका
गीतहरूको बिलौना।

एउटा वाक्य-
बाँकी रहन्छ
“हामी एउटा सपना थियौं
जसले आफ्नै देशलाई हरायो।”
र लाग्छ,
देशले हामीलाई होइन,
हामीले देशलाई
हराइरहेको छौँ।

जमैका, न्युयोर्क, जुन २०, २०२५।

बासभका अरू कविता: परम्पराको कारागार · म थर नभएको आत्मा · म प्रश्न सोध्ने माटो · सबै कविता ›

म थरबाट जन्मिएँ - तर थर कहिल्यै मेरो थिएन। त्यो बुवाको थर थियो, बुबाको पनि, हरेक बुबाहरूको इतिहासमा मातृकुल हराइरहेको प्रमाण। किनभने - म होइन, मेरो थर पो थियो यस देशको नागरिता।

म जन्मिँदा -
छाला एउटै थियो,
रगत एउटै,
हाँसो एउटै।
तर धर्म आयो - उसले मलाई
जातमा काट्यो, थरमा टाँस्यो।

उसले भन्यो -
“तिमी यो होइनौ।
तिमी त्यो -
जसले छोएपछि
पानी पनि अछुतो हुन्छ।”
“पवित्रता किन आगोमा नापिन्छ?”
चुलो छोएर कोही किन “दोषी” हुन्छ?

म जन्मिनु
ममाथि थिएन -
म जन्मनासाथ
मलाई थरले बाँध्यो।
म पनि मान्छे थिएँ -
पसिना बगाउने, गीत गाउने,
आँसु झार्ने अनि आँखा देख्ने।

तर तिमीहरूले
मेरा सबै इन्द्रियहरूलाई
अपराध बनायौ।
धर्मले आदेश दियो – “तिमी तल्लो,”
कसरी मानौँ आत्माको पनि थर हुन्छ?

मलाई थाहा छ -
तिमीहरूले मुर्दा
देवता बनाएका छौ।
तिमिहरूका कुनै
भजनको श्लोकले - मलाई चिनेन।
कुनै धर्मग्रन्थले - मेरो हात समातेन।

मैले भगवान चिनेँ -
तिमीहरूका भगवानले पहिले जात खोजे,
को जाने वैकुण्ठ- को सँधै नरक।

म थरबाट जन्मिएँ -
तर थर कहिल्यै
मेरो थिएन।
त्यो बुवाको थर थियो,
बुबाको पनि,
हरेक बुबाहरूको
इतिहासमा मातृकुल हराइरहेको प्रमाण।

किनभने -
म होइन, मेरो थर पो थियो
यस देशको नागरिता।

कसरी मानौं -
कि म पापी हुँ?
म यो थर लिएर बाँचें।
यो थर लिएर गरे संघर्ष।
त्यो थर किन -
जन्मदैँ दोष मानियो?

कसरी विश्वास गरौं?
स्नान गर्दा शुद्धि गर्ने पानी
मैले छुँदा तिमीलाई अपवित्र लाग्छ?

धारमा एउटै घाम पर्छ,
शरीर एउटै रगतले भरिन्छ।
तर जातको पर्खाल उचालेर
हाम्रो हाँसोमा सिउरिइन्छ।

शब्दमा जस्तो लाज
धर्ममा उस्तै मौनता -
त्यही मौनता जसले
हामीलाई जातको- अन्धकारमा गाड्यो,
जहाँ धर्म एक भ्रम, र अधर्म नै परम्परा।

स्कुल भर्ना फर्ममा -
सबैभन्दा पहिलो प्रश्न
“तपाईंको जात?”

स्कुलको पर्खालमा लेखिएको थियो:
“शिक्षा सबका लागि!”
तर शिक्षकले नाम लिँदा,
उसको नामसँगै जात टाँसिन्थ्यो -
“कामी, दमाई, सार्की…”

आजभोली -
स्कुलमा गुरुले सोधेभने -
“बाआमाको थर के हो?”
म टक्क अडिन्छु,
मैले देवकोटा पढेको छु,
म परिजात सम्झन्छु।

म भनिदिन्छु-
“मेरो थर कविता हो!”
“म थर नभएको आत्मा हुँ,”
“म आत्मा मात्र होइन,
म समाजको सम्पूर्ण रचना हुँ।”

मैले लेखिदिन्छु-
मेरो थर कविता
यो थर- मेरो विरासत होईन,
यो थर- मेरो विरोध हो।

तर यहाँ -
साहित्यमा पनि थर छ, शब्दमा पनि चुलो छ
जसले मलाई सँधै छायाँमा लेखिरहन्छ।

अब बोल्ने पालो मेरो हो।
म लेख्छु -
पर्खालमाथि होइन,
पर्खालभित्रका चिसा
आत्माहरूका लागि।

मेरो कवितामा जात छैन,
वर्ग छैन, पुर्खा छैन, भक्तिभाव छैन,
तर कवितामा आफ्नै अनुहार भेटिन्छ।

तर आज म लेख्छु -
मेरो रगत कुनै देवताको देन होइन,
म तिनै देवतालाई झक्झकाउने कविता हुँ।
म बगाउँदिन शब्दहरू
सस्तो क्रोधमा।
म चलाउँदिन जिब्रो
बिना विवेकको नारा जस्तै।

अब भाषामा मात्र बोल्दिन,
सांसमा बोल्छु - रगतमा बोल्छु,
तिमीहरूले हेपेका ती सबै आंखाको
त्यो नीलो भैसकेको मौनता बोल्छु,
जहाँ जात छैन,
केवल आँखा छन् - साधारण आँखा।

शिव, बुद्ध, र कालो पृथ्वी -
तिमीहरूको मौनताले
मलाई शब्द दियो।
आज जब म कथा सुनाउँछु -
शिवको, रामको, बुद्धको।
म उनीहरूलाई पुछेर,
नयाँ अनुहार दिन्छु,
जहाँ ती देवताहरू मेरो आवाज सुनेर
अलिकति थर्किन्छन्, अलिकति लजाउन्छन।

हे आकाश,
तँ न कुनै थरको होस्
न कुनै वर्णको।
तँजस्तो शून्य,
म पनि तँ बन्न चाहन्छु।

अथवा -
त्यो अन्तिम धूवाँजस्तो,
जातरहित।

म चाहन्छु -
मेरो थर तिमीहरूको मौनता चिरेर
तिमीहरूकै मनको भित्तामा कुँदियोस
एक आगोको अक्षरजस्तो।

बासभका अरू कविता: बुद्ध वाज बर्न इन नेपाल · परम्पराको कारागार · देश हराएको सपना · सबै कविता ›

ऊ गलत जन्मिएको हो, ऊ पसिना भएर बाँच्छ, उसको नाम गलत, जात गलत, रगत गलत, छायाँ अपवित्र। आफूले बनाएको मुर्ती सजिएको मन्दिरको, ढोकामा परम्पराले लेखिदिएको छ - “अछुतलाई प्रवेश निषेध।”

उनीहरू भन्थे -
ईश्वरले बनायो जात।
ईश्वर त बोल्दैन,
लेख्दैन,
गाली गर्दैन।
उ मौन थियो -
जब हातहरूले
“शूद्ध” को छाला चिर्दै,
को- छुत
को- अछुत
आफूखुसी लेखे।

शिव ध्यानमा थिए,
ब्रह्मा कल्पनामा,
विष्णु निद्रामा।
त्यही बीच,
एक पण्डितले बनायो जात,
एक शासकले दियो स्वीकृति,
परम्परा लादेर बनाइए नियमहरू।

ऋग्वेदका मन्त्रहरू
जातको गन्धमा भिज्न थाले।
कविता होइन, आदेश बनाइयो
कसले पढ्न पाउने?
कसले मात्र सुन्न?
कसलाई छुन हुने,
कसले छोए नरक-वास।

कसैले प्रश्न गरेनन् -
किन ब्रह्माले चार वर्ण बनाए?
किन कोही टाकुरा चहार्ने
कोही सधैं भूमिमा थिचिने?

के रगतले जात छुट्ट्याउँछ?
कि ढोंगले?
कि संकोचले?
तिमीहरू भन्छौ -
संसार त नियमले चल्छ,
“हामीले परम्परा छाड्न हुन्न।”

धर्म त उसैले बनायो,
जो डराउँथ्यो परिवर्तनसँग।
जात जन्मिएन,
जात निर्माण भयो -
सत्ता र भयको यन्त्रालयमा।

मन्दिर बनायौ -
तिमी जसको
पूजा गर्छौ -
त्यो देवता,
उसको हातले बनाएको
माटोको मुर्ति हो।

उसले बनाइदिएको
भगवानको नीलो मुर्ति-
अघि घुँडा टेकेर
तिमी धूप बाल्छौ,
अर्घ चढाउछौ,
नतमस्त उभिन्छौ,
हात जोड्छौ।

तर तिमीहरूका -
देवताको आँखामा
उसको छायाँ बिझीहरयो,
घण्ट बनाउने उसका हातलाई
प्रसाद चाख्न प्रतिबन्ध गरियो।

ऊ गलत जन्मिएको हो,
ऊ पसिना भएर बाँच्छ,
उसको नाम गलत,
जात गलत,
रगत गलत,
छायाँ अपवित्र।

आफूले बनाएको मुर्ती
सजिएको मन्दिरको,
ढोकामा परम्पराले
लेखिदिएको छ -
“अछुतलाई प्रवेश निषेध।”

मलाई थाहा छ -
तिमी हलो समाउन्नौ,
खेत जोत्नेलाई ‘हली’ भन्छौ,
उसले फलाएको अन्न चाहिन्छ।
उसको अन्न फलाउने हातले,
बार्दली नाँघेर कहिल्यै
तिमीहरूको भान्सा नटेकुन।

कति सस्तो छ तिमीहरूको भय?
के ऊसले पानी छोयो भने
तिमीहरूको ईश्वर मर्छ?
के उसको छायाँ परेको खाना खाए
तिमिहरूको नरकवास हुन्छ?

मैले आर्यघाटमा
देखेको छु- दुई शब।
एउटा चढेको बाँसमा,
अर्को- ट्रकको छायाँमा।

एउटा -
“पण्डितको बाउ,”
अर्को -
“चर्पी सफा गर्नेको आत्मा”।
दुवैका आमा रोएकै थिइन्
एकै रङको रुवाईमा।

दुबै जले - एउटै माटोमा,
एउटै घाट - “दुई जात।”
राग एउटै, धूवाँ एउटै,
मर्म एउटै, शोक एउटै।

मैले प्रस्न गरेँ -
“कसले बनायो जात?”
"हे मानव!
किन अझै किन बाँधिन्छौ
भित्रभित्रै चिटिक्क,
धर्मको रेसा बुनेर?”

मैले सोधे -
तर मेरो प्रश्न
“पवित्रता भन्दा भयानक।"
“धर्म तोड्ने” ठहरियो।
किनकि -
जात भनेको धर्मको ज्वरो हो,
न निको हुन्छ,
न आफैं सकिन्छ।

अब
लेखनु छ नयाँ वेद,
नयाँ पुराण -
जहाँ शिवले डमरु दलितसँग बजाउँछन्,
सरस्वतीले सबैका स्वर गान्छिन्।
जहाँ जात छैन -
छ केवल आत्माको उज्यालो र छायाँ।

बासभका अरू कविता: मानुषी: भुपीसँगका थाँती संवाद · बुद्ध वाज बर्न इन नेपाल · म थर नभएको आत्मा · सबै कविता ›

हरेक शब्दमा, बिस्ट्याउँछौं, एके-४७ का बारुदहरू, हरेक भावहरू, ओतप्रोत हुन्छन्, लोभले, ईर्ष्या ले, घिनले, घमन्डले, अनि खोक्रो आत्मसम्मानले, थाह छैन- कसैलाई, कर्मको, बुद्धको मर्मको, को छ हिँडेको- साँच्चीकै, बुद्धले देखाएको…

हरेक शब्दमा,
बिस्ट्याउँछौं,
एके-४७ का बारुदहरू,
हरेक भावहरू,
ओतप्रोत हुन्छन्,
लोभले, ईर्ष्या ले,
घिनले, घमन्डले,
अनि खोक्रो आत्मसम्मानले,
थाह छैन- कसैलाई,
कर्मको,
बुद्धको मर्मको,
को छ हिँडेको- साँच्चीकै,
बुद्धले देखाएको बाटोमा?
संसारिक जन्जालमा जेलिएर,
ईर्ष्या, राग, अनि फुस्रो घमन्डका,
गोला बारुदले भरिएको,
ज्यानलाई डोर्याउँदै,
उक्लन्छौं,
स्वयम्भूका डाँडा,
डुल्छौं,
बौद्धका गल्लीहरू,
वर्षमा एक दिन,
आजै,
जन्माउन बुद्धको जन्मजयन्ती,
अनि भन्छौं,
ह्यासट्याग मा राखेर,
#BuddhawasBornInNepal
बुद्ध नेपालमा जन्मेको हो।
हरे मुर्ख नेपाली हो,
बुद्ध जन्मिँदैनन्,
यौटा राजकुमार जन्मेको थियो,
बाँचो,
आफनै कर्मले,
ज्ञानको ज्योती पायो,
बुद्धत्व पायो,
बोधिसत्व भयो
भने बुद्ध.. बस।

बासभका अरू कविता: म, तिमी, हामी · मानुषी: भुपीसँगका थाँती संवाद · परम्पराको कारागार · सबै कविता ›

भुपी, हिजो तिमीले तिम्रो चोकमा रोग, भोक र शोक देख्यौ, “देशको नाभी” त्यही चोकमा आज धेरै थोक थपिएको छ। ती चोकहरूका भित्तामा, पुरुषहरूले इतिहास लेख्दै गर्दा, टाउकोमा पानीको घाम बोकेर कविताको छायाँ बनेर बाँचिरहेकी मानुषी…

भुपी,
हिजो तिमीले तिम्रो चोकमा
रोग, भोक र शोक देख्यौ,
“देशको नाभी” त्यही चोकमा
आज धेरै थोक थपिएको छ।
ती चोकहरूका भित्तामा,
पुरुषहरूले इतिहास लेख्दै गर्दा,
टाउकोमा पानीको घाम बोकेर
कविताको छायाँ बनेर
बाँचिरहेकी मानुषी देखेनौँ,
उसको शरीर देखेनौँ,
उसको आत्माको चित्कार
के तिमीले देख्यौ
त्यो चोकको छेउमा
चुपचाप टोलाउँदी मानुषी?
उसको स्वर तिम्रा कविताबाट
किन कहिल्यै फुत्किएनन्?

उ मानुषी,
उ पनि त त्यही चोककै थिई।
उ न त कवितामा पसी
न मन्दिरको देउतामा।
के तिमीले त्यो चोकमा
उसको आवाज सुनेका थियौ, भुपी?

तिमी शहीदको गणना गरिरह्यौ,
तर सुनेनौ विस्थापित सपनाहरू,
दिनदिनै बरबराउने
मानुषीको मौनता -
शब्दहीन, इतिहासविहीन।

भुपी,
तिमीले त लेख्यौ–
“म चोकमा बस्दछु,”
तर ऊ त त्यस चोकमै हराइरहेकी थिई।
शब्दहरू लेख्न सक्नेहरूले
कति सजिलै पचाइदिन्छन्
अदृश्य अन्याय?

भुपी, मलाई जवाफ चाहिएको छ -
किन उसको हाँसो कहिल्यै
तिम्रो चिया बोटहरूमा फक्रेन?
किन उसको उपस्थिति -
सधैं ओझेल, सधैं पृष्ठभूमि?
कविता बन्न नसकेकी इतिहास?

भुपी -
के बुझ्यौ कहिलेकाहीँ,
अल्झिएको हाँसोभित्र
चर्को चित्कार लुकेको हुन्छ?
हिजो तिमीले पनि त उसको
अनुहार चिनेका थियौ -
उसको आँसु बुझेका थियौ कि?

आज ऊ मानुषी -
बाँचिरहेकी छे
बहिरा कान र बन्द आँखाबीच।
इतिहासले लेखिरहन्छ -
पुरुषले देख्ने, पुरुषले भोग्ने,
पुरुषले व्याख्या गर्ने दुःख।

म मानुषी -
तिमी यो चोकको कवि थियौ,
म - यो चोकको साक्षी।
तिमी बस्यौ कविताको साथ,
अहिले म यो चोककी निवासी -
बिनाशब्दका घाउ बोकेर
टोलाउँदै, टुक्रिँदै
घण्टाघरको फेदमा उभिएर
रानीपोखरीको रित्तोपनजस्तै
समय उल्टिएको हेरिरहेकी छु।

कविता किन बोल्दैन, भुपी?

म मानुषी -
कहिले भित्तामा झुन्ड्याइएकी चित्र,
कहिले नारी दिवसको भाषण।
तिमीहरूले मलाई चिनेका थियौ,
तिमीहरूले मलाई नियालीरहेका थियौ -
मेरो शरीरको हरेक चाल, हरेक कमजोरी।
नदेखिएको त वर्षौँदेखिको दोहन छ,
नसुनिएको त मजस्ताका चित्कार छन्,
नलुटिएका त मेरो जस्तै मौनता छन्,
नखोसिएको त सास मात्रै छन्।

तिम्रो चोकले - तिम्रा कविताहरूले
सुनेनन् - म मानुषीको मौन चित्कार।

म मानुषी -
अब म तिम्रो
कविताको पात्र होइन,
आफ्नै कथाको लेखिका।
मैले देखेको छु -
तिमीहरूको इतिहासमा,
तिमीहरूको कृति‌हरूमा -
राजा, कवि, शासक, र विद्रोही।

तर म?
म त केवल प्रसंग थिएँ -
कहिले दुःखको, कहिले प्रेमको,
तर कहिल्यै निर्णयको होइन।

तिमीले रङ देख्यौ झण्डामा,
मैले रगत देखेँ
आफ्नो शरीरबाट बगिरहेको।

तिमीले भन्ने गर्थ्यौ “देश”
तर त्यो देश
मेरा लागि कहिल्यै घर भएन।

मलाई त तिमीहरूको
वंशावलीमा पनि ठाउँ भएन।

म मानुषी,
अब मलाई तिमीहरुको कविता होइन,
मेरो आफ्नै स्वर चाहिएको छ।
अब म लेख्दैछु नयाँ इतिहास -
म पुरुषहरूको आँखामा प्रश्न राखिदिन्छु -
किन युद्ध सधैं पुरुषका नाममा हुन्छ?
किन वीरगति पाउनेहरूलाई
सधैं पुरुषत्व चाहिन्छ?
किन बलिदान स्त्रीको हुन्छ,
तर श्रेय पुरुषको?

तिमीहरू सधैं भन्थ्यौ -
“युग बदल्न कविहरू चाहिन्छ।”
जो कवितामा चुपचाप आत्मा लुकाउँछन्
र हाँस्दा आँसु पखाल्छन्?

अब म भन्छु -
युग बदल्न कवयित्रिहरूको क्रोध चाहिन्छ।

मेरो कविताहरू कराउनेछन् -
तोड्छन्, खण्ड–खण्ड पार्छन्
र फेरि बनाउँछन् नयाँ ढाँचा।

भुपी,
अब म मैनवत्तीजस्तो जल्दिन -
म आगो बन्छु, र जलाउँछु
इतिहासका ती पृष्ठ,
जहाँ मेरा कथा कहिल्यै लेखिएनन्।

title.$t: Hippies: Music, Marijuana, Magic Bus and Kathmandu

content.$t:
The Road to Freak Street: How Kathmandu Briefly Became the Last Stand of Hippie Culture

From Haight-Ashbury and Woodstock to the Magic Bus and Freak Street: how Kathmandu became the last stop of the hippie dream, and how it ended.

A revised and fact-checked version of an essay first posted on Kafkaintherun in April 2025.

The Eden Hashish Centre, the best known of Kathmandu’s government-licensed hashish shops, in June 1973, a few weeks before Nepal revoked every cannabis licence. Photo: Roger McLassus, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (cropped).

“If you’re going to San Francisco / Be sure to wear some flowers in your hair.

If you’re going to San Francisco / You’re going to meet some gentle people there.”

—Scott McKenzie, “San Francisco” (1967)

In the summer of 1967, the air was thick with incense, rebellion, guitars and drums. A strange and beautiful migration was underway. Young people from across America poured into San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury neighborhood, holding peace signs, dressed in tie-dye, humming Jefferson Airplane and Dylan, quoting Ginsberg, Kerouac and Alan Watts. Chanting “Turn on, tune in, drop out,” they came chasing a free spirit. That summer—now immortalized as the Summer of Love—gave the world a movement that would ripple across continents: the hippies.

Who were the hippies? Ask anyone, and you will probably hear about strangely dressed young people with long hair, unshaven beards and beads, flowers pinned to tie-dyed shirts, eyes hazy with marijuana, acid and other drugs. Ask someone who knows a little more, and they will tell you about a generation that wanted a world where people could live together without fighting one another, a generation that sang of war and peace and raged against age-old systems.

In short

  • The hippie movement grew out of Thoreau and the Beat poets and burst into view in 1967, with the Summer of Love and the Monterey Pop Festival, and then at Woodstock in 1969.
  • As the dream soured at home, young Americans and Europeans took the overland Hippie Trail from London or Amsterdam through Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan to Kathmandu.
  • Kathmandu’s Freak Street (Jhochhen Tole) was the last stop, home to guesthouses, pie shops and government-licensed hashish shops such as the Eden Hashish Centre.
  • Nepal revoked every cannabis licence in July 1973 and passed the Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act in 1976. In 1979 the Iranian revolution and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan closed the road.
  • The spirit moved on to Thamel, where trekking replaced tripping.

I grew up hearing stories about the hippies and the Magic Buses that brought them to Kathmandu. The stories came from fathers and uncles of that generation—men who started smoking weed, or started wearing jeans and bought guitars and dreamy jackets, after meeting the hippies in the early 1970s.

Roots of the Revolution: Thoreau to the Beat Generation

The hippie movement didn’t begin with guitars and acid trips. Its roots go deeper—into the pages of Thoreau’s Walden. “Simplify, simplify,” wrote Thoreau, who left society to live in a cabin in the woods by Walden Pond, in search of simplicity, self-reliance and harmony with nature—values the hippies would later make their own. His Civil Disobedience taught a future generation to resist; Walden taught it to listen to the language of trees. A century later, the Beat writers—Kerouac, Ginsberg, Burroughs—picked up the torch in the smoky cafés of New York and San Francisco, seeking enlightenment through Zen, jazz and the open road. The Beatniks became the spiritual ancestors of the hippies, and Bob Dylan’s “The Times They Are a-Changin’” gave the next generation its anthem.

By the mid-1960s, the stage was set. The Beat spirit fused with the civil rights movement, the protests against the Vietnam War, and a growing mistrust of government that began with the Cuban Missile Crisis and Kennedy’s assassination—a mistrust that Martin Luther King Jr.’s murder in 1968 would only deepen. The young answered with an idealistic new order: psychedelics, free love, communal living and the wisdom of the East. The hippies were not simply escapists. They were idealists rebelling against a segregated, mechanized world, and their existential search eventually led many of them down the mystical paths of the East.

Music: Shaped the Movement and Shocked the World

Music was the movement’s heartbeat. Scott McKenzie’s “San Francisco” played like a sacred invitation. “Be sure to wear some flowers in your hair,” he sang, inviting the world into a moment of collective transcendence. That same summer, the Beatles released Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band and sang “All You Need Is Love” live to a worldwide television audience. “A splendid time is guaranteed for all,” they promised. It was a promise of freedom, a utopia of music, art and mind expansion—a world that felt both distant and close, like a dream on the verge of becoming real.

In the Panhandle of Golden Gate Park, the Grateful Dead, Jefferson Airplane and Big Brother and the Holding Company, with a young Janis Joplin, played free concerts off the backs of flatbed trucks. Timothy Leary, who had made “Turn on, tune in, drop out” famous at the Human Be-In that January, kept chanting his LSD slogan. Young people from all over America converged on Haight-Ashbury, a neighborhood named after the corner of Haight and Ashbury streets. They came for escape and the expansion of consciousness, for music, for peace and protest, for grass and acid. That summer, Haight-Ashbury gave its name to the Summer of Love, and the hippie era had begun.

Young hippies on Haight Street, in an Associated Press photo printed on April 30, 1967, weeks before the Summer of Love. Source: The Greenville News / AP, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

San Francisco was not the only place where the counterculture took shape in 1967. That June, the Monterey International Pop Festival—America’s first large-scale rock festival—gave the psychedelic movement, already brewing in San Francisco’s acid tests and be-ins, its first great stage. Pink Floyd were still a London underground band, unknown in America, but Grace Slick was there with Jefferson Airplane, whose “White Rabbit” had turned Alice in Wonderland into an acid trip. Eric Burdon’s new Animals and The Who thrilled the crowd with new sounds. Jimi Hendrix set his guitar on fire, and Janis Joplin poured out her raw soul, both announcing themselves to the world as never before. The old guard was changing, and a new kind of music was being born.

An advertisement for the Monterey International Pop Festival, with the lineup, the arena seating plan and ticket prices, from the June 3, 1967 issue of KRLA Beat. Source: KRLA Beat, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

This was also when America discovered the music of the East. On the last afternoon of the festival, Ravi Shankar, with Alla Rakha on tabla, held the arena spellbound with his sitar for close to three hours. When he finished, the stunned crowd rose in an ovation whose echoes still reverberate.

Woodstock: The Ultimate Expression of Peace and Protest

By August 1969, all these ideas collided in a way no one had expected, least of all the organizers. Nearly half a million people—musicians, activists, seekers, young people from all over America—gathered on Max Yasgur’s dairy farm in Bethel, New York, for Woodstock, a festival of peace, love and music. There were no borders, only blankets, bodies, guitars and endless smoke. For three electric days, Woodstock was a utopia: muddy, chaotic and peaceful, utterly human and beautiful. The hippie dream seemed real, if only for a fleeting moment.

The whole event teetered on collapse, yet somehow held together long enough for dozens of acts, each offering its own sonic vision of freedom, rebellion and soul. Richie Havens opened with improvised urgency, strumming “Freedom” until his fingers bled and setting the tone for what became a four-day odyssey of music and mud. Santana, then a little-known San Francisco band, delivered a volcanic “Soul Sacrifice” that catapulted them into legend.

Saturday afternoon at Woodstock, August 16, 1969: the crowd on its feet after a set by a band most had never heard of, which was Santana. Photo: James M Shelley, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Deep into Saturday night, Janis Joplin sang the blues like a soul on fire. At dawn on Sunday, after The Who had left the stage, Grace Slick woke those who had never slept, promising “morning maniac music” as Jefferson Airplane began their set. Later, Joe Cocker turned the Beatles’ “With a Little Help from My Friends” into a gospel sermon, and Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young nervously admitted, “This is the second time we’ve ever played in front of people,” before delivering harmonies that sounded like fragile prayers. But the undisputed star was Jimi Hendrix. Delays pushed his closing set to Monday morning, when only about 40,000 people remained. In a red headband and a white fringed jacket, he tore into a distorted, metallic “Star-Spangled Banner,” turning the national anthem into what many heard as a protest against the Vietnam War.

Woodstock was more than music. It was a temporary nation of barefoot idealists and muddy prophets, held together by shared hope, shared danger and shared dreams. Joni Mitchell, who missed the festival and watched it on television from a New York hotel room, captured the feeling perfectly in her song “Woodstock”:

“We are stardust, we are golden / And we’ve got to get ourselves back to the garden.”

The Decline in the 1970s: A Move to the East

But utopias rarely last, and that garden was never really found. The festival ended, and the idealism faded. Four months later, at Altamont, a young man was stabbed to death in front of the stage. Within a year of the 1970s arriving, Jimi, Janis and Jim Morrison were all dead. The new political reality of Richard Nixon replaced the dreamy haze of the sixties. Drug laws hardened into a War on Drugs, the war in Vietnam spilled into Cambodia and Laos, and the cultural backlash came banging on the door. What had been a movement began to feel like a memory. As the decade turned, the music, the movement and the spirit drifted outward—toward the mythical East.

The garden, it seemed, had not been regained; it had been paved over. What began as a spiritual rebellion was now being sold on cereal boxes and department-store racks. And so many young Americans and Europeans—disillusioned, restless, still searching—did something radical: they left. They left behind the suburbs and the strip malls and followed the rising sun. They turned East, toward India, Afghanistan and, finally, Nepal. Toward mystics, mountains and myths. Into the unknown.

The garden, it seemed, had not been regained; it had been paved over.

The Hippie Trail

As the Western dream turned sour, a new pilgrimage took shape: an overland route from Europe across Asia that ended in Kathmandu, the last sanctuary on the road to spiritual awakening. From London to Kathmandu, the Hippie Trail became a rolling confession, a drifting escape, a rite of passage. Some rode the Magic Bus and its many rivals—rickety, colorfully painted coaches that carried travelers from London or Amsterdam to Kathmandu for less than a hundred pounds, cheap for a journey across half the world. Others drove VW vans, squeezed onto local buses or simply hitchhiked.

The usual path:

London/Amsterdam → Istanbul → Tehran → Herat → Kabul → Khyber Pass → Peshawar → Lahore → Delhi → Varanasi → Kathmandu (with Goa as the beachside detour)

The overland Hippie Trail, from Istanbul through Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan to India and Kathmandu. Map: NordNordWest, CC BY-SA 3.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons.

We picture one particular Volkswagen as the Magic Bus, but it was never a single bus. It was a symbol of the journey: slow, chaotic and full of adventure.

In Tehran, Herat, Kabul and Peshawar, travelers met an Islamic world that, in many ways, no longer exists. In Goa, they danced to sitars and the sea. In Rishikesh and Varanasi, they chanted with sadhus in the ashrams. But in Kathmandu, they found the mythical last stop. In place of Woodstock’s crowds, there were temple bells, the smoke of incense and hashish, and silent meditation. Some came chasing nirvana, others narcotics; most sought escape. The East promised what the West had failed to deliver: peace, mysticism and freedom—real or imagined.

The Pudding Shop in Istanbul, where overland travellers met, swapped tips and pinned notes to its board before heading east; here in 1982, a few years after the trail closed. Photo: Mike McBey, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
Some came chasing nirvana, others narcotics; most sought escape.

Kathmandu: A Himalayan Shangri-La at the End of the Road

Before the buses arrived in droves, Kathmandu in the 1960s was already a whispered legend among seekers and drifters. A handful of adventurers—explorers, artists, musicians, poets—made their way to the Himalayas, drawn by tales of a medieval city untouched by time, where temples outnumbered cars and marijuana grew wild along the riverbanks.

Kal Bhairav in Kathmandu Durbar Square, photographed by a traveller in December 1972. Photo: MauriceJFox3, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons.

Kathmandu soon collected rock-and-roll legends of its own. Allen Ginsberg spent 1962 and 1963 wandering India, and his fellow Beat poet Gary Snyder made it to Kathmandu. In Jomsom, in Mustang, a trekkers’ lodge still offers guests the chance to stay in “the same lodge as Jimi Hendrix,” and a scrawl on its wall is signed “Jimi Hendrix Jomsom Oct. ’67.” It is a lovely legend, though in October 1967 Hendrix was busy touring Europe, and the line above the signature borrows from “Voodoo Child (Slight Return),” a song he had not yet recorded. Janis Joplin never made it to Nepal, but in “Cry Baby” she sang that “the road’ll even end in Kathmandu.” Cat Stevens sang of “Katmandu” in 1970, and Bob Seger turned it into a rock anthem in 1975 without ever setting foot here. Years later, John Lennon, who had gone to India with the Beatles in 1968, slipped “a little yellow idol to the north of Katmandu” into “Nobody Told Me,” borrowing the opening line of a 1911 music-hall poem, “The Green Eye of the Little Yellow God.”

The early visitors were not tourists. They were pilgrims of the mind, in search of something sacred—Buddhism, hashish or just silence—and Nepal, opened to foreigners only in the 1950s, offered all three. The air was thin, the pace unhurried, and the line between sacred and profane was blurry. Marijuana was not just legal; it was sold in government-licensed shops, alongside postcards, prayer beads and colorful clothes. Kathmandu became a quiet Eden, a Shangri-La in the Himalayas.

By the early 1970s, the whispers had become a roar. This potent blend of the sacred and the remote drew a new kind of traveler. Kathmandu was the final stop on the Hippie Trail, a high-altitude utopia where marijuana was legal, the people were kind and the soul could rest. They came in waves—by bus, in VW vans or simply by hitchhiking—carrying guitars, notebooks, dreams and tales. On the quiet banks of the Bagmati or in the echoing courtyards of Patan, many Westerners believed they had found what America’s cities and communes had promised but never delivered: a culture steeped in ritual, yet open to wanderers.

For travelers, Kathmandu was cheap, welcoming and otherworldly. Many wandered through the monasteries of Boudhanath and Swayambhu, meditating quietly with monks. Others found refuge in the temples of Pashupatinath, more enchanted than devout. In Bhaktapur and Patan, they painted, photographed and sketched, mesmerized by the medieval architecture and a pace of life that felt untouched by time. A few settled for weeks on the outskirts—in Nagarkot, Pharping and Shivapuri—camping under the stars on the hilltops, reading Hesse and the Gita. They were not tourists; they were dwellers and seekers, drawn to ritual and reverie, chasing stillness through pujas and a hashish haze, often blurring the line between reverence and indulgence.

Freak Street: The Epicenter of Hippies in Nepal

At the center of it all was Freak Street—Jhochhen Tole—a short, stone-paved lane just south of Kathmandu Durbar Square. What had been a quiet residential alley turned, almost overnight, into a global crossroads of wanderers, mystics, artists and seekers. Guesthouses sprang up in old brick buildings, serving as both meeting places and refuges for the travel-weary. The newcomers brought guitars, poetry, incense and questions. In return, they found a culture steeped in centuries of spirituality, hospitality and patience. And at the heart of the street were the licensed hashish shops, the most famous of them DD Sharma’s Eden Hashish Centre, whose yearly calendars travelers carried home as souvenirs.

The menu board of the Eden Hashish Centre in 1973, offering “first quality” hash and ganja, temple balls, hashish oil and hashish cake. Photo: Richard Weil, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

On Freak Street, guitars mingled with Tibetan horns. Pie shops and chai houses sprouted like mushrooms, and menus offered ganja milk tea and hashish-laced eggs. Record players spun Dylan and Donovan under prayer flags. Here, you could trade your jeans for a homespun robe and spend your afternoons reading Ginsberg or Rimbaud. As the sun dipped behind the temple rooftops, you might find yourself invited to an impromptu sitar concert or one of countless bhajan sessions. For a time, Freak Street was not just a place but an idea: freedom, escape, and the hope that somewhere between East and West, a new self might be born.

For a time, Freak Street was not just a place but an idea: freedom, escape, and the hope that somewhere between East and West, a new self might be born.

For a brief window, Nepal did not just host the global counterculture; it shaped its myth. Kathmandu became a meeting point between ancient ritual and Western rebellion, between spiritual tradition and psychedelic experiment. It was not always harmonious, but it was undeniably transformative. Kathmandu offered something profoundly different: space to breathe, reflect and heal.

War on Drugs: The End of the Beginning and the Garden Lost

Then the dream began to unravel. In July 1973, under pressure from the United States and the United Nations, Nepal revoked every cannabis license, and the hashish shops, symbols of Kathmandu’s permissiveness, closed almost overnight. The Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act of 1976 made the ban law. Visa rules grew stricter, and the cafés thinned out. Then 1979 closed the road itself: revolution in Iran and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan cut the overland route, and the last buses stopped running. Kathmandu’s days as a sanctuary for the global counterculture were over.

Jars on the counter of a Kathmandu hashish shop in 1973, the year the licences were revoked. Photo: Richard Weil, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

But something lingered. The hippies left Freak Street, but their footprints did not fade so easily. In guesthouses and trekking agencies, German bakeries and reggae bars, that era still echoes in today’s Thamel. The ethos of alternative living, global curiosity and spiritual seeking survived, migrating from Jhochhen to Thamel, from hash pipes to hiking boots. Trekking replaced tripping. The Kathmandu Valley, once a canvas for psychedelic dreams, became a launchpad for commercial adventure. Nepal adapted, and moved on.

Freak Street (Jhochhen Tole) in 2009: the name survives on the signboards. Photo: Holynow, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

And yet, for those who remember it, or inherited the memory, the hippie era remains suspended in Kathmandu’s smoke-framed nostalgia. Freak Street was never just an idea; it was a place where the dreams of the 1960s could linger a little longer, and its imprint never really faded. Through the 1980s and ’90s, its influence echoed in Kathmandu’s bohemian corner cafés and in a new generation of musicians and writers. Even today, when tourists arrive with trekking poles rather than tie-dye, the spirit of those years survives in subtler ways: in Kathmandu’s tolerance for wanderers, and in its fusion of the sacred and the everyday.

Perhaps the garden was never meant to be found. But for a brief moment, Kathmandu felt like a place where it almost could be. The hippie movement did not change the world the way its idealists had hoped. It did not end war or dismantle capitalism. But it left behind something perhaps even more valuable: the idea that a different world was possible, one where love, music and freedom were the ultimate expressions of life.

Frequently asked questions

What was Freak Street in Kathmandu?

Freak Street is the nickname of Jhochhen Tole, a short lane just south of Kathmandu Durbar Square. In the late 1960s and early 1970s it was the hub of the hippie scene, full of cheap guesthouses, pie shops, chai houses and government-licensed hashish shops such as the Eden Hashish Centre.

When did Nepal ban marijuana and hashish?

In July 1973, under pressure from the United States and the United Nations, Nepal revoked all cannabis licences and the hashish shops closed. The Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act of 1976 made growing, selling and using cannabis a crime.

What was the Hippie Trail?

An overland route that young Western travellers followed from the 1960s until 1979, from London or Amsterdam through Istanbul, Tehran, Herat, Kabul, the Khyber Pass, Peshawar and Lahore to Delhi, Varanasi and Kathmandu, often by bus, van or hitchhiking.

Did Jimi Hendrix ever visit Nepal?

There is no evidence that he did. A lodge in Jomsom, Mustang, shows graffiti signed “Jimi Hendrix Jomsom Oct. ’67”, but in October 1967 Hendrix was touring Europe, and the line borrows from “Voodoo Child (Slight Return)”, a song he only recorded in 1968.

Why did the Hippie Trail end?

In 1979 the Iranian revolution and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan closed the overland route. By then Nepal had also banned cannabis, and cheap flights were replacing the long road east.

title.$t: On This Tiny pale blue Dot, Why Such Deep Divides?

content.$t:
If there is a creator of this universe, wouldn’t they belong to the whole cosmos, not just our tiny corner? In the grand scale of things, what are our prayers? Would this cosmic god be pleased with or endorse, what…

“On the scale of the cosmos, human divisions seem absurd. Yet, here on our ‘Pale Blue Dot,’ the poison of caste discrimination continues to inflict deep wounds, particularly in societies like Nepal.”

A Pixel Suspended in a Sunbeam

In 1977, NASA launched two spacecraft- Voyager I and II- on, what was initially a five-year mission to explore our solar system. Their task was to study planets, take pictures, and record atmospheric data of the outer planets of our solar system. More than four decades later, both Voyagers are still flying, journeying into the unknown, far beyond Pluto, into the deep and silent cosmos. But Voyager 1 ended up doing something much bigger than science- it helped us see ourselves differently. Before Voyager 1’s camera went dark forever at Sagan’s urging; it turned back for one last look at Earth.

In February 1990, as Voyager 1 approached the edge of our solar system- about 6 billion kilometers away from the sun- it turned its camera back toward Earth one last time. Mission managers, at the suggestion of Carl Sagan, asked the spacecraft to take one final photograph before turning its camera off forever to save the energy of Voyager I for the journey to deep space.

What came from that moment was not just a scientific image- it was a philosophical revelation. Voyager 1 snapped a mosaic of 60 photos that became known as the first “family portrait” of our solar system. In one of those images, Amid the vast darkness, Earth appeared as a mere glint, barely a pixel, suspended in a sunbeam.

Sagan famously called it “The Pale Blue Dot,” and in his book, Pale Blue Dot: A Vision of the Human Future in Space, he wrote:
“Look again at that dot. That’s here. That’s home. That’s us. On it everyone you love, everyone you know, everyone you ever heard of, every human being who ever was, lived out their lives……”

Earth appeared as nothing more than a “tiny blue speck of light,” less than a pixel wide, caught in a beam of sunlight.

To me, this remains one of the most humbling and powerful images humanity has ever taken. It showed how small and fragile our Earth is- not just in our solar system, but in the unimaginable vastness of the universe. Most of the stars we see in the night sky are either distant galaxies or long-dead suns. The light we receive from them takes millions of years to reach us, many of these stars are long dead before their light reaches us. In such a massive scale, how important- or rather, unimportant- are the boundaries we draw between us?

When confronted with the scale of the universe—trillions of stars, billions of galaxies- I found it humbling to consider how insignificant our daily conflicts and egos must appear.

A Cosmic God and Our Earthly Boundaries

A little disclaimer- I don’t believe in a god anymore. I gave up believing when my dear friend was diagnosed with leukemia at the age of 14. But I have chased spirituality, read many myths and books, and tried to understand what we humans hope for in the divine.

If there is a creator of this universe, wouldn’t they belong to the whole cosmos, not just our tiny corner? In the grand scale of things, what are our prayers? Would this cosmic god be pleased with or endorse, what we’ve done in their name- wars, hatred, discrimination, and division?

We may never find the answer to that, but one thing is certain: this Pale Blue Dot is the only home we have. Eight billion of us, cohabiting with millions of other species, all our history, dreams, failures, and future- everything we are- sharing one planet, sharing one future. And yet, caste-based discrimination, rationalized by appeals to tradition, religion, and inherited power structures, remains a blight on our society.

Why do we, priding ourselves on intelligence, cling so fiercely to these irrational divisions – by caste, ethnicity, gender, or religion? Why is divinity so often invoked to justify hate and hierarchy? Who someone marries, where they live, what they eat, or what job they do- why are these things still grounds for judgment?

From Ancient Texts to Modern Tragedies

Nowhere is this more painfully manifest than in our caste system. While its origins are debated, its formalization, many believe, was cemented by texts like the Manusmriti. The Vedic concept of varnas, perhaps not originally hierarchical, arguably became distorted over time, codified into rigid stratification based on birth, purity, and notions of superiority.

I don’t know exactly how caste-based discrimination began in our society, but like many, I believe it was formalized through ancient texts- especially the Manusmriti, which turned what may have started as occupational divisions into rigid, inescapable social hierarchies. The Vedas had varnas, and perhaps the original intention wasn’t to discriminate. But the Upanisads and Purans slowly embedded the idea that Brahmins and Chettris are somehow superior. Manusmriti turned that idea into law. And today, many of us still follow it- not as law, but as word of God.

Though outlawed by our constitution, these ideas persist as deeply ingrained, often unquestioned, ‘tradition.’ The brutal 2020 killings of Nabaraj Bika and his friends in Rukum West, and the death of Angira Pasi in Rupandehi, are horrific recent reminders. Their alleged crime? Daring to love across caste lines. These tragedies provoked outrage, but often only fleetingly. In a context where caste-based violence remains tragically normalized, such incidents struggle to maintain public attention. The cycle repeats.

Why is a life from a so-called ‘Dalit’ community still implicitly valued less than a ‘Bahun’ life in practice?

Growing Up Inside the Shadows of Caste

Growing up, my first experience with caste discrimination came from reading Muna-Madan. I couldn’t understand why a Chettri had to kneel to a Brahmin. Why was it taboo for a Darjee woman to ask for dahi at our home? “Everyone says your curd is delicious, wish I could have some too,” Thuldidi once told my grandmother. I remember asking my grandfather why she couldn’t have it, like others did. As a child, I didn’t have the words or courage to protest- but I knew something was wrong.

When Sunil, my friend, came to visit, certain rooms were off limits. We ate outside. He was never invited to our puja or family functions. Years later, when Gyanu sir- our teacher- ate lunch with us in the kitchen, Budathokii Aamai was scandalized. “Kaami can change his name to B.K., but he will always be Biswakarma,” she muttered. That stigma doesn’t go away just because someone changes their surname. I’ve seen change, yes. My family, too, has grown more accepting. But the shadows of old beliefs linger, the deep-rooted stigma doesn’t vanish easily.

Even in love, caste finds its way in. When I broke up with someone from the Shrestha community, my grandmother was happy. She didn’t hide it. I still don’t know what hurt more- the heartbreak or her reaction. “Don’t fall in love with a girl from pani nachalne jaat,” my mother once said. Her concern wasn’t the girl, it was the fear of society- the priest refusing to perform funeral rites, the gossip, the boycott. Even now, my mother cautions me against marrying someone from a so-called “untouchable” caste- not because she believes in these divisions, but because she fears what society will say, what the priests will do, and whether our neighbors will boycott us. This fear, this silent complicity, sustains the system.

Beyond the Constitution: Why Silence Is Not Enough

We’ve come far, but not far enough. Yes, caste-based discrimination is illegal. But laws don’t change societies overnight. Change is slow. Too slow. It took generations before someone like Gyanu Sir could be seen as an equal at our table. It took 128 generations of Khatiwada to finally let Gyanu sir eat at our dining table. Even then, it felt like a rare exception- not a new normal. But it happened. And that proves it can happen again.

The law may prohibit caste-based discrimination, but law alone is not enough. We have come a long way from the past generations, it is “illegal’ to discriminate anyone based on religion, gender, caste, culture or race according to our constitution. Has the law worked? Certainly Not. Will the law work? The society is deep-rooted in centuries of oppression and supremacy that it will take time. What good is a constitution if society refuses to evolve with it? How long? Hopefully next generation or soon? Real change comes not only from awareness but from action.

Nabaraj and Angira, and so many of us are still preyed like second class citizen, a stupid sense of false narcissism. I shouldn’t be afraid to follow what my heart wants just because a relative-aunt or a priest might decide so. Sunil can come inside my house if he wants to. Thuldidi can taste the curd that we make. I don’t have to think of Gyanu sir dining with us as a special occasion. Will the priests allow ‘a daughter-in-law of lower caste’ to be part of ‘upper caste in law’s’ funeral? Will Thuldai stop standing last in the queue to offer Shivaratri prayers in the temple in our village.

I’ve always considered myself someone who doesn’t discriminate. But is that enough? Is staying silent the same as staying neutral? Why haven’t I done more? Why haven’t we?

Getting to the root of centuries of discrimination is certainly not easy, and it takes much more than one informed person. We must ask ourselves: how many of us have spoken up to our families, our neighbors, when they say something discriminatory? How many of us have told our Thuldai that he doesn’t have to stand last in line for Shivaratri puja?

Just knowing that something is wrong is not enough. Tolerance is not enough. We must act. We cannot wait for the next generation. Change doesn’t begin “someday.” It begins with us. Now.

To all the gods, myths, and cosmic forces watching this Pale Blue Dot- we are not hopeless. We can change. We must.

Not as Bahuns or Dalits.
As Nepalis.
As humans.
